assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting changed how trade is theorized, measured and taken to firm-level data. It shifted the field's focus from sectors to firms and gave a new account of the gains from trade through reallocation and productivity selection. Its reach into macro, growth and productivity is broad.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central model. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, and his broader theory of trade with differentiated products and organization, round out the core. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are important parallel contributors outside the credited set. Redding's later quantitative and spatial work is valuable but less central to this specific discovery.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation in firm microdata across many countries, and the framework is standard in graduate teaching and policy analysis. The timing is not premature.
uncertainties: The Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum contribution limits a clean two-person attribution.
Helpman's other work (trade and organization, political economy of protection) might make a different framing preferable.
Krugman's earlier prize covered part of the new-trade-theory lineage.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Sufficient-statistics methods and empirical estimation of behavioral responses to taxation have reshaped optimal tax theory and applied public finance. Policy relevance is very high. Methodological innovation (bunching, administrative data, sufficient statistics) is influential well beyond public economics.
assessment.attribution: Saez is central through optimal tax formulas linked to elasticities and top-income taxation. Chetty is central through the sufficient-statistics approach and identification with administrative data. Slemrod's contributions to taxable-income elasticities and tax avoidance are substantial, and Stantcheva's are more recent. Feldstein's seminal elasticity-of-taxable-income work cannot be credited. Mirrlees's earlier prize covers the theoretical foundations.
assessment.maturity: The core contributions are 15 to 25 years old and widely replicated or extended. Some of Chetty's agenda is still young, but the tax-response and sufficient-statistics work is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with other Saez and Chetty candidacies (inequality, mobility) complicates how the prize is framed.
Debates over the size of taxable-income elasticities persist.
The best-fitting trio or pair is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with nominal rigidities, microfounded Phillips curves and the analysis of interest-rate rules, underpins modern central-bank practice and monetary theory. Its influence on policy and on the DSGE toolkit is very large.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main problem. Woodford's systematic theory of monetary policy and Gali and Gertler's New Keynesian Phillips curve and policy-rule work are the most coherent trio. Calvo (pricing), Taylor (rules and staggered contracts), and Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (medium-scale DSGE and identification) are also major. Any three-person selection leaves out others. Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Phelps and Taylor-style contributions have partly been honored already.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of use. Questions raised by the 2008 crisis and the post-2021 inflation episode have not undermined the framework, though they have prompted refinements such as heterogeneous-agent extensions.
uncertainties: Eight credited names show diffuse credit and make a three-person cap difficult.
Taylor and Calvo may have a stronger priority claim than the proposed trio.
The post-2021 inflation episode and HANK developments may shift the field's assessment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators are among the most used tools in applied empirical work in growth, development, finance and industrial organization. The methods addressed a pervasive practical problem and enabled credible estimation with lagged dependent variables and fixed effects.
assessment.attribution: Arellano-Bond (1991), Arellano-Bover (1995) and Blundell-Bond (1998) form the core. Anderson-Hsiao and Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen are precursors, and Hansen's GMM is the general foundation, already honored. Blundell's wider contributions to microeconometrics add to his case but are not specific to this item.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. Known issues such as instrument proliferation and weak instruments have been documented and have not diminished its standing.
uncertainties: Methodological prizes are sometimes judged to be less urgent.
Overlap with other Blundell candidacies (B049).
Proliferation of instruments and misuse in applied work complicate the evaluation of impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation research program offered a quantifiable, firm-level account of why aggregate productivity differs across countries. It links microdata to macro development accounting and has generated a large literature on frictions, policy distortions and reallocation.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the pivotal paper. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) is a parallel and equally foundational contribution, and Restuccia is credited but Rogerson is not. The set is therefore incomplete, and a two-person selection omits Restuccia. Banerjee-Duflo and Jovanovic-style antecedents also matter.
assessment.maturity: The framework is about 15 years old, widely applied and also criticized (measurement error, markup versus distortion interpretation). The evidence base is large but still being debated.
uncertainties: I disclose a research relationship with Klenow (a long-running collaboration), so this assessment should be weighed accordingly.
Measurement-error critiques may limit how literally the TFP-loss magnitudes can be taken.
The Restuccia-Rogerson attribution gap complicates the choice of laureates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Task-based accounts of technology and the China trade shock changed understanding of labor-market polarization, local adjustment and the distributional costs of globalization. They have had a major effect on policy debate and empirical practice.
assessment.attribution: The China shock papers by Autor, Dorn and Hanson are a clear unit. Autor's task-based work with Katz, Levy and Murnane and with Acemoglu belongs to the broader theme, and Acemoglu's prize in 2024 partly covers task-based theory. Katz's contribution is major but would require a different framing or a larger group.
assessment.maturity: The core China-shock research is about a decade old. Evidence is extensive, but debates continue about long-run persistence, magnitudes and design choices, and the follow-up literature is still developing.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the task-framework work already acknowledged in the 2024 prize.
Persistence and magnitude of the effects remain debated.
Katz is a major contributor who would be omitted from a three-person selection.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design supply a unified framework for how a sender can optimally shape information. It has proven useful across mechanism design, regulation, communication and market design. The conceptual contribution is clean and general.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica-Gentzkow (2011) is the origin. Bergemann and Morris developed the broader information-design and Bayes correlated equilibrium framework. A three-person limit forces a difficult choice among the four credited names. Gentzkow's empirical media work is additional, but it is a separate topic.
assessment.maturity: The field is roughly 15 years old and growing quickly. It has great theoretical influence but less empirical or policy validation than others on the list, so the timing may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: The empirical and policy impact is still limited compared with older candidates.
Choosing three of four credited names is difficult.
Antecedents in cheap talk and signaling mean a priority argument is possible.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The microfoundations of agglomeration (sharing, matching, learning), the economics of cities and the empirical measurement of density effects are central to understanding productivity, growth and spatial inequality. Policy relevance for housing, land use and regional development is high.
assessment.attribution: Duranton-Puga's microfoundations survey and Glaeser's empirical and conceptual work on cities and human capital are core. Moretti (local multipliers and spillovers) and Gyourko (housing) are strong contributors. Fujita, Krugman and Venables (new economic geography) are partly covered by Krugman's earlier prize. The lineage is diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Decades of empirical confirmation, though identification of agglomeration elasticities remains difficult. The field is mature and ongoing.
uncertainties: Diffuse credit across five credited names.
Causal identification of agglomeration effects remains debated.
Overlap with trade and geography prizes already awarded.
